::: {.quip}
Don't repeat yourself — unless it's the final check.
:::

## What I did

- **Linear algebra by hand**: caught up on two weeks at once — six sessions on determinants, complex numbers, Cramer's rule, and some trigonometry along the way.
- **The Linux Command Line**: chapters 14–17, which completes the first two parts of the book.
- **Rosalind**: CONS, Consensus and Profile — building a profile matrix from several DNA strings and reading the most common letter at each position.
- **Academic Vocabulary in Use**: units 2–5, with new words added to my flashcards.

## What clicked

- Complex numbers in determinants. For a matrix with c + di and c − di in the corners, the product of these two numbers turned out to be just a difference of squares: (c + di)(c − di) = c² − (di)² = c² + d², because i² = −1. A complex number times its conjugate is a plain real number. Once I saw that, determinants with i stopped looking scary.
- Writing code once and reusing it. For CONS I needed to read FASTA files, so I wrote my own parser and moved it into a separate module. Now every new Rosalind problem starts with one `import` line instead of copying the same code again.

## Where I got stuck

- Small signs, big errors. I kept writing i² as 1 instead of −1, which flipped the sign of a whole term in the determinant. In the linear systems I solved with Cramer's rule, the final check didn't match because of a single sign.
- Brute-force Python. My CONS solution works, but it's long and repetitive. I can see that it could be shorter (for example, with `zip` or `lambda`), but I'm not at that level of Python yet.
- FASTA format. One sequence can be split across several lines, and at first it wasn't obvious how to glue the lines back into a single string.

## What I'm changing

- Always substitute the answer back into the original equations — the check catches exactly the sign mistakes I keep making.
- Practice Python idioms (`zip`, dictionaries, `lambda`) on small exercises, so that my Rosalind solutions become shorter over time.
- Keep a growing module of my own utilities and reuse it.
